questions.stem: A parent asks whether aspirin should be given to a 10-year-old with fever during a suspected viral illness. Which response is most appropriate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Avoid aspirin in children and adolescents with suspected viral illness because of the association with Reye syndrome","B":"Use aspirin as the preferred first-line antipyretic because viral illness does not alter its pediatric safety profile","C":"Double the usual aspirin dose because higher dosing reduces the risk of neurologic complications during influenza","D":"Aspirin is appropriate whenever fever exceeds 38.5°C because the Reye-syndrome warning applies only to adults"}}
questions.rationale: Aspirin and other salicylate-containing products should generally be avoided in children and adolescents during influenza, varicella, or other suspected viral illness because of the association with Reye syndrome. The original item was tightened to avoid making an unnecessary blanket claim about specific substitute antipyretics.
questions.source_name: FDA — Required Warning for Aspirin-Containing Drug Products
questions.source_detail: Pediatric viral-illness warning regarding Reye syndrome

questions.stem: An adult has a deep contaminated puncture wound and an unknown tetanus vaccination history. Which prophylaxis should the nurse anticipate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A tetanus-toxoid-containing vaccine plus tetanus immune globulin, along with appropriate wound care","B":"Systemic antibiotics alone because antibiotics replace tetanus vaccination and immune globulin after contaminated wounds","C":"Wound cleansing alone because an unknown vaccination history is treated as proof of a complete primary series","D":"No tetanus prophylaxis unless clinical tetanus develops because puncture wounds are classified as clean minor wounds"}}
questions.rationale: CDC classifies penetrating or puncture wounds as dirty or major wounds. For a dirty or major wound with unknown vaccination history, tetanus vaccination is indicated and TIG is also indicated. Antibiotics are not recommended solely to prevent tetanus.
questions.source_name: CDC — Clinical Guidance for Wound Management to Prevent Tetanus
questions.source_detail: Dirty/major wound prophylaxis with unknown vaccination history

questions.stem: Which instruction is correct for use of an epinephrine auto-injector during anaphylaxis?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Inject into the anterolateral thigh and follow the specific device instructions for activation and hold time","B":"Inject into the abdomen because abdominal tissue provides the recommended emergency absorption site","C":"Avoid use through clothing under all circumstances because clothing always prevents delivery of epinephrine","D":"Delay injection until a clinician can confirm the allergen because early epinephrine is contraindicated in suspected anaphylaxis"}}
questions.rationale: Epinephrine auto-injectors are intended for intramuscular or subcutaneous administration into the anterolateral thigh. Device-specific instructions must be followed because activation and hold times differ among products. Many products permit use through clothing when necessary.
questions.source_detail: Recommended anterolateral-thigh administration and product-specific instructions

questions.stem: Which statement about home insulin storage is correct?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Unopened insulin is generally refrigerated, while allowable room-temperature storage after opening depends on the specific product label","B":"Insulin should be frozen whenever possible because freezing extends potency beyond the labeled expiration date","C":"Insulin may be stored in direct sunlight as long as the cap remains on the vial or pen","D":"All insulin products have identical room-temperature stability periods, so product-specific labeling does not need to be checked"}}
questions.rationale: FDA notes that manufacturers generally recommend refrigerated storage for insulin and that unopened refrigerated products retain potency to the labeled expiration date. Room-temperature allowances vary by product, so the specific label should be followed; insulin should not be frozen or exposed to excessive heat.
questions.source_name: FDA — Information Regarding Insulin Storage and Switching Between Products in an Emergency
questions.source_detail: Refrigerated storage and labeled room-temperature allowances

questions.stem: A chemotherapy drug is classified as a vesicant. What is the key implication if the drug extravasates into surrounding tissue?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"It can cause severe local tissue injury, including blistering, ulceration, or necrosis depending on the agent","B":"It causes only transient discomfort because vesicants cannot produce tissue necrosis after extravasation","C":"Its effects are exclusively systemic, so the infusion site does not require assessment during administration","D":"It is interchangeable with a nonvesicant irritant because both terms indicate the same degree of tissue injury"}}
questions.rationale: Vesicants are agents capable of producing substantial local tissue injury after extravasation, potentially including blistering, ulceration, and necrosis. This distinguishes them from agents that are irritants without the same necrotic potential.

questions.stem: A client reports tremor and a rapid heartbeat after using inhaled albuterol. How should the nurse interpret these findings?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"They are recognized adverse effects of beta-adrenergic agonist therapy and should be assessed for severity and persistence","B":"They prove the medication is ineffective and require the client to double the next dose without further assessment","C":"They are unrelated to albuterol because inhaled beta agonists cannot produce systemic cardiovascular or neuromuscular effects","D":"They always indicate anaphylaxis and therefore establish a diagnosis of severe allergic reaction without other findings"}}
questions.rationale: Albuterol labeling describes tremor and cardiovascular effects including tachycardia/palpitations. These may occur with beta-adrenergic stimulation and should be interpreted in clinical context rather than automatically treated as treatment failure or allergy.

questions.stem: When rotating a client from one opioid to another, what is the purpose of an equianalgesic estimate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"To estimate relative analgesic potency as a starting point, followed by a safety reduction and individualized titration when switching opioids","B":"To establish an exact milligram-for-milligram dose that can be transferred directly between all opioids without adjustment","C":"To eliminate the need to consider incomplete cross-tolerance, organ function, route, or individual response during the switch","D":"To determine only nonopioid analgesic doses because equianalgesic concepts are not used when comparing opioid potency"}}
questions.rationale: Equianalgesic tables estimate relative opioid potency but are not exact conversion targets. When switching to a different opioid, the calculated equivalent is generally reduced to account for incomplete cross-tolerance and individual variability, then titrated to clinical response.
questions.source_name: CDC Clinical Practice Guideline for Prescribing Opioids for Pain — 2022
questions.source_detail: Cautions on opioid conversion and incomplete cross-tolerance

questions.stem: A client is stopping long-term proton pump inhibitor therapy after the prescriber confirms there is no continuing indication. Which teaching is accurate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Transient upper gastrointestinal symptoms can occur from rebound acid hypersecretion after discontinuation","B":"Stopping a PPI permanently suppresses gastric acid, so rebound symptoms cannot occur after discontinuation","C":"A PPI must always be tapered because abrupt discontinuation is prohibited by current expert guidance","D":"Any symptoms after stopping prove that the original diagnosis was incorrect and require permanent PPI therapy"}}
questions.rationale: AGA guidance advises that patients discontinuing long-term PPI therapy may experience transient symptoms from rebound acid hypersecretion. Importantly, either tapering or abrupt discontinuation can be considered, so the original claim that abrupt cessation itself is inappropriate was too strong.
questions.source_name: American Gastroenterological Association — Clinical Practice Update on De-Prescribing PPIs
questions.source_detail: Rebound acid hypersecretion; tapering or abrupt discontinuation may be considered

questions.stem: A client is about to start atorvastatin. Which liver-related monitoring statement is accurate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Consider liver-enzyme testing before initiation and repeat testing later when clinically indicated","B":"Routine weekly liver-enzyme testing is required for every client throughout atorvastatin therapy","C":"Liver enzymes should never be checked because atorvastatin has no recognized hepatic adverse effects","D":"Serum calcium is the primary laboratory test used to detect atorvastatin-related hepatic injury"}}
questions.rationale: Current atorvastatin labeling advises considering liver-enzyme testing before initiation and when clinically indicated thereafter. The original item incorrectly implied routine ongoing liver-enzyme monitoring solely because of a family history of liver problems.
questions.source_detail: Hepatic dysfunction warning and liver-enzyme testing guidance

questions.stem: A client with heart failure who is receiving high-dose diuretic therapy is starting lisinopril. Which effect requires particularly close monitoring when therapy is initiated?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Symptomatic hypotension, especially when diuresis has contributed to volume or sodium depletion","B":"Marked hypertension because ACE inhibition typically causes an abrupt increase in systemic vascular resistance","C":"Hyperglycemia because severe glucose elevation is the principal first-dose effect of lisinopril","D":"No hemodynamic effect because diuretic therapy eliminates the blood-pressure response to ACE inhibition"}}
questions.rationale: Lisinopril can cause symptomatic hypotension. Labeling identifies heart failure, high-dose diuretic therapy, and severe volume or salt depletion among risk factors for excessive hypotension, so close monitoring is appropriate when therapy is initiated in such patients.
questions.source_detail: Hypotension risk with heart failure, high-dose diuretics, and volume/salt depletion
